query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy, the presence of the fifth element increases local lattice distortions and promotes enhanced short‐range chemical order that raises the barriers for dislocation glide compared to its quaternary and ternary subsets, thereby producing higher yield strength and a more pronounced work hardening response.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC alloys produced by identical thermomechanical processing—one being the full quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the others being equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
generation.intervention: Systematically remove one or two constituent elements from the quinary alloy while preserving the single-phase FCC structure.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compression tests) performed under the same strain rate and temperature conditions (room temperature and/or cryogenic temperature), ensuring identical processing histories.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion fields and localized chemical short-range order.
generation.mechanism: In the quinary alloy, the additional compositional complexity increases local stress field fluctuations (due to greater atomic size and modulus mismatches) and promotes SRO formation, which together impede dislocation motion (e.g., causing rugged, stepped dislocation paths and requiring higher stresses for glide). In contrast, the quaternary and ternary variants, having reduced compositional complexity, exhibit less lattice distortion and weaker SRO, leading to lower barriers for dislocation movement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will display lower yield strength and reduced work hardening rates, with microstructural features showing smoother dislocation glide and diminished evidence of deformation heterogeneities (such as wider dislocation separation or fewer pinned segments).
generation.baseline: The mechanical properties (yield strength, work hardening rate, dislocation behavior) observed for the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy under controlled thermomechanical processing.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when all alloys remain in a single-phase FCC structure with comparable grain sizes and processing histories; extremes in testing temperature (where thermal activation might override lattice effects) may obscure the predicted differences.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence points to lattice distortion and SRO as plausible mediators, the relative quantitative contributions and interactions with other factors (e.g., stacking fault energy changes) are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of alloys consisting of the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets using identical thermomechanical processing to ensure a single-phase FCC structure. Subject these alloys to mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or compression tests) at controlled temperatures (room and cryogenic temperatures) and strain rates. Simultaneously, use in situ TEM or high-resolution electron microscopy and atom probe tomography to characterize dislocation behavior and local chemical ordering.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate from stress–strain curves
Dislocation mobility characteristics (e.g., glide roughness, pinning events)
Signatures of short-range ordering or lattice distortions (via TEM/atom probe)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quinary alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength and work hardening (or show evidence of more impeded and fluctuating dislocation motion correlated with enhanced SRO/lattice distortion) compared to the quaternary and ternary alloys under identical testing conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

In addition to twinning activities and GPFE curves, we further investigated the dislocation morphology and mobility at a constant strain rate or shear stress, with results indicating that there was a higher barrier for achieving equivalent dislocation velocity in HEAs than in Ni (Supplementary Fig. 9). The extended dislocation in HEA exhibited rugged dislocation lines and a significantly varied dissociation width, which differed markedly from that in Ni with smooth straight dislocation lines and a uniform SF width. Dislocation glide in the HEA was enabled via a series of forward slips by local segments after depinning from local heterogeneities,, and this resulted in nontrivial fluctuations in shear stress under a constant strain rate or in dislocation velocity under constant shear stress. The distinct dislocation behavior of the HEA is essentially pertinent to the severe lattice distortion due to the different atomic sizes and intrinsic properties of individual constituent elements,. Tests in the polycrystalline single-phase state have shown that CrMnFeCoNi exhibits certain noteworthy mechanical properties, including significant temperature dependence of yield stress coupled with moderate strain-rate sensitivity at low homologous temperatures, and positive correlation between strength and ductility, and strength and toughness at cryogenic temperatures. These features cannot be easily modeled in terms of the behavior of simple FCC solid solutions given that there are no “solvent” or “solute” atoms in equiatomic alloys. Although, in principle, the temperature dependence of yield stress (increasing strength with decreasing temperature) implies some sort of thermally activated process of yielding, the fundamentals of solid-solution hardening and plastic deformation have not yet been fully characterized or quantified. This is due in part to the difficulty of obtaining large single crystals of the HEA. Only very recently has a paper been published on the growth and compression testing of a bulk single crystal of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA; however, just one loading axis [51] was tested and the authors did not perform any dislocation analysis.

Recently, Ding et al. synthesized FCC CoCrFeNiPd and CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. The former exhibited a higher yield strength than the latter with comparable tensile ductility. They proposed that the essential difference between these two HEAs was associated with atomic segregation and short-range ordering (SRO); both were enhanced in CoCrFeNiPd, as compared with CoCrFeNiMn. The idea was that SRO tends to create resistance to deformation/slip, leading to larger dislocation glide resistance in the more ordered CoCrFeNiPd than in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Theoretical work by Yin et al. suggested that the strengthening was due mainly to the large atomic/misfit volume of Pd in CoCrFeNi. Ma et al. identified a number of unusual features associated with dislocations/slips in HEAs that were related to lattice distortion and/or local chemical order. SRO also occurs in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The atomic structure of a CoCrNi MEA indicates that Cr favors Ni and Co neighbors, reducing the electrical and thermal conductivities and increasing the stacking-fault energies and hardness.
